opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to look at it historically. In OpenAI's early days, reinforcement learning was the main bet. There was Gym, the Dota project, the robotic hand solving the Rubik's cube. The belief was that if you set up the right environment and the right reward, an agent would learn through trial and error and eventually become intelligent.

Those projects were impressive, but they shared a limitation: the agents were very good at one thing and didn't generalize. A Dota agent can't write an email. The missing piece wasn't the RL algorithm; it was the prior, the general knowledge about the world and language that lets you transfer across tasks.

GPT filled that gap. Pretraining on huge amounts of text gives you a model with broad priors, and once you have that, RL becomes much more meaningful. So I don't see the GPT turn as OpenAI abandoning RL. It's more that they found the ingredient RL was missing. First came RLHF, which was a fairly light use of RL, mostly about alignment and making the model helpful and follow instructions. Then came reasoning models, where RL is used more seriously: you let the model think, try things, and get rewarded on verifiable outcomes like math or code.

One way I like to put it: language is the key that makes RL generalize. When an agent can reason in language, its "actions" include thinking, and thinking transfers across environments in a way that pressing buttons in a game doesn't.

So in their strategy, RL went from being the whole story, to being a finishing step, and now back to being central, but sitting on top of a pretrained foundation. I think the more interesting question now is less about the algorithm and more about environments and evaluation. What tasks do we put these models in, and how do we define reward for things that are useful in the real world but hard to verify? That's where a lot of the next progress will come from.

r001.rationale: It says GPT did not mean OpenAI abandoned RL, and describes RL shifting from the whole strategy to a role built on pretrained foundations.

r002.rationale: It describes RLHF as helping with alignment and instruction-following, but does not state that RLHF was necessary for ChatGPT to become a product.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the interesting thing about OpenAI is that it actually started as a reinforcement learning company. If you look at the early years, the work was Gym, the Dota project, the robot hand, all of this was RL. The founding belief was that agents learning from reward in environments would be the path to AGI. And then GPT came along, and for a while it looked like RL got pushed aside, because the thing that scaled was next-token prediction on internet text. You just pour in more data and compute, and the model gets better. That's a very different philosophy from RL, where you need an environment and a reward and a lot of careful engineering.

But I don't think RL ever really left. It changed form. The first place it came back was RLHF. GPT-3 was impressive, but it was hard to use. It would complete your prompt rather than answer your question. RLHF, which became InstructGPT and then ChatGPT, was what turned a language model into something people could actually talk to. So RL was the thing that made the product possible, even though pretraining was the thing that made the capability possible. That division of labor is important. Pretraining gives you the prior, the knowledge, the world model. RL gives you the behavior, the objective, the alignment with what people want.

And then the more recent phase, which I think is the one that matters most, is RL for reasoning. With the o-series, you're no longer just using RL to shape style or politeness. You're using it to make the model think longer and better, to learn from whether the answer was actually right. That's a return to the original OpenAI idea, but with a key difference. The agent now comes with a huge prior from pretraining, so it doesn't have to learn everything from scratch inside the environment. That's what made RL hard before. Exploration was impossible without a prior. Language models solved that.

So my understanding is that the strategy was never pretraining versus RL. It was a sequence. Pretraining first, because that was what scaled. Then RL on top, because once you have a good prior, RL becomes extremely data-efficient and you can optimize for things that really matter, like correctness on hard problems or completing a task in a real environment. I'd say the next few years are mostly about the second half of that sequence. The question is no longer whether RL works for language models. It's what environments and what rewards we build, because that's what decides what these models actually get good at.

r001.rationale: The response says RL never left and describes the strategy as a sequence: pretraining first, then RL on top. This frames GPT’s rise as a shift in emphasis, not abandonment of RL.

r002.rationale: It says RLHF turned the language model into something people could talk to and made the product possible.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish reinforcement learning as a research direction from reinforcement learning as a stage in building a model. As GPT became the focus, pretraining gave us a very powerful starting point: a model with broad knowledge and capabilities learned from text. Reinforcement learning could then help turn those capabilities into behavior that is useful for a particular objective.

So I wouldn’t interpret the shift toward GPT as abandoning reinforcement learning. It changed where RL fit. Instead of learning everything from scratch through interaction, you could start with a pretrained model and optimize how it responds or acts. Human feedback is one way to provide that signal; tasks with verifiable outcomes offer another.

The interesting question then becomes: what can the model learn through actually trying things and receiving feedback that it cannot learn just by predicting text? That is especially relevant for reasoning and agents, where success depends on a sequence of decisions. From that perspective, GPT and reinforcement learning are complementary parts of the strategy.

r001.rationale: It says GPT did not mean abandoning RL and that RL’s role changed, but does not characterize the shift as a reweighting of research investment.

r002.rationale: It mentions human feedback as one possible signal, but does not state that RLHF was necessary for ChatGPT to become a product.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that, as GPT became a major focus, reinforcement learning increasingly became a way to turn a pretrained model’s capabilities into useful behavior. Pretraining gives you a strong starting point, but predicting the next token doesn’t directly tell the model how to respond to a user, solve a task, or make a sequence of decisions.

RL provides a way to optimize for those outcomes. With human feedback, the signal can be whether an answer is helpful. For tasks where you can check the result, it can be whether the model actually succeeds. So I see GPT and reinforcement learning as complementary: GPT provides the foundation, and RL helps shape what the model does with it. That becomes especially interesting when you move from generating a response to taking actions and learning from their consequences.

r001.rationale: It describes GPT and reinforcement learning as complementary but does not say OpenAI reweighted research investment toward GPT or that RL was not abandoned.

r002.rationale: It mentions human feedback as an RL signal, but does not state that RLHF was necessary for ChatGPT to become a product.
